summary.text: Writing the coefficient as \(\prod_{k<n}\frac{3(9k+2)(9k+4)(9k+7)}{(k+1)^2(3k+1)}\), the proof shows its \(3\)-adic valuation is \(n-2v_3(n!)\ge0\) by the standard factorial-valuation bound. For each prime \(p\ne3\), valuations are expanded into divisibility counts modulo every \(p^j\); choosing \(y\equiv-9^{-1}\pmod{p^j}\) identifies the relevant residue classes, and a finite analysis of \(9y+1=mp^j\) shows that the three numerator-class counts dominate the count for \(3k+1\) plus twice that for \(k+1\), so all prime valuations are nonnegative and the rational number is integral.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(x)={}_3F_2\!\left(\frac29,\frac49,\frac79;\frac13,1;729x\right)
      =\sum_{n\geq 0}A_nx^n.
\]
We prove that every coefficient \(A_n\) is an integer.

Recall that the coefficient of \(z^n\) in
\({}_3F_2(a,b,c;d,e;z)\) is
\[
 \frac{(a)_n(b)_n(c)_n}{(d)_n(e)_n}\frac1{n!},
\]
where \((u)_n=u(u+1)\cdots(u+n-1)\). Since \((1)_n=n!\), we obtain
\[
 A_n=729^n
 \frac{(2/9)_n(4/9)_n(7/9)_n}{(1/3)_n(n!)^2}.
\]
Now
\[
 (a/9)_n=9^{-n}\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(9k+a),\qquad
 (1/3)_n=3^{-n}\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(3k+1).
\]
Because \(729=9^3\), the three factors \(9^{-n}\) cancel \(729^n\), while division by \((1/3)_n\) contributes \(3^n\). Thus
\[
 \boxed{
 A_n=
 \frac{3^n\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(9k+2)(9k+4)(9k+7)}
 {\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(3k+1)\,(n!)^2}.}
 \tag{1}
\]
In particular \(A_0=1\), and taking the quotient of consecutive terms gives
\[
 A_{k+1}=A_k\,
 \frac{3(9k+2)(9k+4)(9k+7)}{(k+1)^2(3k+1)}.
 \tag{2}
\]
All factors here are positive and nonzero. This also shows directly that the rational sequence defined by this recurrence is precisely the coefficient sequence of the stated hypergeometric series.

We prove integrality prime by prime. For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(t)\) for the usual \(p\)-adic valuation of a nonzero integer or rational number. From (1), additivity of valuations gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(A_n)
 ={}&n v_p(3)
 +\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\bigl(v_p(9k+2)+v_p(9k+4)+v_p(9k+7)\bigr)\\
 &-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_p(3k+1)-2v_p(n!).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]
We will show that this is nonnegative for every prime \(p\).

## The prime \(p=3\)

None of \(9k+2,9k+4,9k+7,3k+1\) is divisible by \(3\). Hence (3) reduces to
\[
 v_3(A_n)=n-2v_3(n!).
 \tag{4}
\]
If \(n=0\), this is zero. If \(n>0\), Legendre's elementary bound
\[
 (p-1)v_p(n!)\leq n-1
 \tag{5}
\]
holds for every prime \(p\). For completeness, it follows from Legendre's formula
\[
 v_p(n!)=\sum_{i\geq1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\]
and the estimate
\[
 (p-1)v_p(n!)
 \leq (p-1)n\sum_{i\geq1}p^{-i}=n;
\]
the left side is a multiple of \(p-1\), and the sharper standard form \((p-1)v_p(n!)\le n-1\) also follows immediately by writing \(n\) in base \(p\), or from
\((p-1)v_p(n!)=n-s_p(n)\) with digit sum \(s_p(n)\ge1\). Taking \(p=3\) gives
\[
 2v_3(n!)\le n-1<n,
\]
so (4) is nonnegative.

It remains to handle primes \(p\ne3\). The main ingredient is a counting argument modulo each power of \(p\).

## Valuations as divisibility counts

For every positive integer \(x\),
\[
 v_p(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbf 1_{p^j\mid x},
 \tag{6}
\]
because \(p^j\mid x\) holds exactly for \(1\le j\le v_p(x)\). All sums in (6) are finite. Also
\[
 v_p(n!)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_p(k+1).
 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently, to prove that the part of (3) not involving \(n v_p(3)\) is nonnegative, it is enough to establish, for every \(j\ge1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\#\{0\le k<n:p^j\mid9k+2\}
 +\#\{0\le k<n:p^j\mid9k+4\}\\
&\qquad
 +\#\{0\le k<n:p^j\mid9k+7\}\\
&\hspace{20mm}\ge
 \#\{0\le k<n:p^j\mid3k+1\}
 +2\#\{0\le k<n:p^j\mid k+1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, summing (8) over \(j\), and using (6) and (7), gives exactly the required valuation inequality.

If one wants a common explicit finite range for this summation, take
\(B=9n+8\). Every positive number occurring for \(0\le k<n\), namely
\(9k+2,9k+4,9k+7,3k+1,k+1\), is less than \(B\). Thus each valuation can be written as the sum of its divisibility indicators for \(1\le j<B\), with all later indicators zero. This justifies rearranging the finite sums over \(k\) and \(j\).

We now prove (8).

## A residue-counting lemma

Fix an integer \(D\ge2\). For \(0\le r<D\), let
\[
 C_n(r)=\#\{0\le k<n:k\equiv r\pmod D\}.
\]
Writing \(n=qD+s\), where \(0\le s<D\), the first \(qD\) integers consist of \(q\) complete residue blocks, followed by residues \(0,1,\ldots,s-1\). Therefore
\[
 C_n(r)=q+\begin{cases}1,&r<s,\\0,&r\ge s.\end{cases}
 =\left\lfloor\frac nD\right\rfloor+\mathbf 1_{r<n\bmod D}.
 \tag{9}
\]
In particular,
\[
 0\le r\le s<D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_n(r)\ge C_n(s).
 \tag{10}
\]
Thus, among residues in their standard range \([0,D-1]\), a smaller residue occurs at least as often in the initial interval \(0,\ldots,n-1\) as a larger one.

## The relevant residue classes modulo \(D=p^j\)

Fix a prime \(p\ne3\), an integer \(j\ge1\), and put \(D=p^j\). Then \(D\ge2\), and \(9\) is invertible modulo \(D\). Choose the unique representative \(y\), \(0\le y<D\), satisfying
\[
 9y\equiv-1\pmod D.
 \tag{11}
\]
Then, for any integer \(a\),
\[
 D\mid9k+a
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 k\equiv ay\pmod D.
 \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, multiplying the congruence \(9k\equiv-a\) by \(y\), and using \(9y\equiv-1\), gives \(-k\equiv-ay\), hence \(k\equiv ay\). The converse is the same calculation reversed.

In particular, if we denote least nonnegative residues modulo \(D\) by brackets, then
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{divisibility condition}&\text{residue class of }k\\ \hline
D\mid9k+2 &[2y]\\
D\mid9k+4 &[4y]\\
D\mid9k+7 &[7y].
\end{array}
\tag{13}
\]
For \(3k+1\), note that \(3\) is also invertible modulo \(D\), and
\[
D\mid3k+1
\Longleftrightarrow D\mid3(3k+1)=9k+3
\Longleftrightarrow k\equiv3y\pmod D.
\tag{14}
\]
Finally,
\[
D\mid k+1\Longleftrightarrow k\equiv D-1\pmod D.
\tag{15}
\]
Therefore (8) will follow if
\[
 C_n([2y])+C_n([4y])+C_n([7y])
 \ge C_n([3y])+2C_n(D-1).
 \tag{16}
\]
By (10), each of \(C_n([2y]),C_n([4y]),C_n([7y])\) is at least \(C_n(D-1)\), because every one of the residues \([2y],[4y],[7y]\) is at most \(D-1\). Hence it remains only to prove that at least one of \([2y],[4y],[7y]\) is at most \([3y]\). Equivalently, we need
\[
 [3y]\ge[2y]\quad\text{or}\quad
 [3y]\ge[4y]\quad\text{or}\quad
 [3y]\ge[7y].
 \tag{17}
\]
Once (17) is known, the numerator residue occurring on its right supplies the \(C_n([3y])\) term by (10), while the other two numerator residues each supply one copy of \(C_n(D-1)\). This proves (16).

## Proof of the residue ordering

It remains to establish (17). Since (11) says that \(D\mid9y+1\), write
\[
 9y+1=mD.
 \tag{18}
\]
The left side is positive, so \(m\ge1\). Since \(y<D\),
\(9y+1<9D\), and hence \(m<9\). Moreover \(3\nmid m\): if \(3\mid m\), then the right side of (18) would be divisible by \(3\), whereas \(9y+1\equiv1\pmod3\). Therefore
\[
 m\in\{1,2,4,5,7,8\}.
 \tag{19}
\]
We check these six possibilities. The following table gives Euclidean decompositions modulo \(D\). The fractions shown are integers because of (18); they lie in \([0,D-1]\), so they are precisely the indicated least residues. Their nonnegativity also follows from the corresponding possible congruence \(mD\equiv1\pmod9\) (and \(D\ge2\)); the upper bound by \(D-1\) is immediate from the displayed numerators.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m&[3y]&\text{comparison residue}&\text{conclusion}\\ \hline
1&\dfrac{3D-3}{9}&[2y]=\dfrac{2D-2}{9}&[3y]\ge[2y]\\[2mm]
2&\dfrac{6D-3}{9}&[7y]=\dfrac{5D-7}{9}&[3y]\ge[7y]\\[2mm]
4&\dfrac{3D-3}{9}&[7y]=\dfrac{D-7}{9}&[3y]\ge[7y]\\[2mm]
5&\dfrac{6D-3}{9}&[4y]=\dfrac{2D-4}{9}&[3y]\ge[4y]\\[2mm]
7&\dfrac{3D-3}{9}&[4y]=\dfrac{D-4}{9}&[3y]\ge[4y]\\[2mm]
8&\dfrac{6D-3}{9}&[4y]=\dfrac{5D-4}{9}&[3y]\ge[4y].
\end{array}
\tag{20}
\]
Here are the decompositions behind the table, to make the modular calculation explicit. From \(y=(mD-1)/9\):

* If \(m=1\), then
  \(3y=(3D-3)/9\) and \(2y=(2D-2)/9\).
* If \(m=2\), then
  \(3y=(6D-3)/9\) and
  \(7y=D+(5D-7)/9\).
* If \(m=4\), then
  \(3y=D+(3D-3)/9\) and
  \(7y=3D+(D-7)/9\).
* If \(m=5\), then
  \(3y=D+(6D-3)/9\) and
  \(4y=2D+(2D-4)/9\).
* If \(m=7\), then
  \(3y=2D+(3D-3)/9\) and
  \(4y=3D+(D-4)/9\).
* If \(m=8\), then
  \(3y=2D+(6D-3)/9\) and
  \(4y=3D+(5D-4)/9\).

In every row, comparison of the displayed remainders proves the stated inequality. Thus (17) holds in all possible cases. As explained above, (17), the monotonicity (10), and the residue identifications (13)--(15) prove (8).

## Completion for primes \(p\ne3\)

For \(p\ne3\), we have \(v_p(3)=0\). Sum inequality (8) over all \(j\ge1\). Using (6), the left side becomes
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
 \bigl(v_p(9k+2)+v_p(9k+4)+v_p(9k+7)\bigr),
\]
and the right side becomes
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_p(3k+1)
 +2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_p(k+1)
 =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}v_p(3k+1)+2v_p(n!).
\]
Comparison with (3) gives
\[
 v_p(A_n)\ge0
\]
for every prime \(p\ne3\). Together with the earlier treatment of \(p=3\), this proves
\[
 v_p(A_n)\ge0\qquad\text{for every prime }p.
\tag{21}
\]

Finally, a rational number is an integer if and only if all its prime-adic valuations are nonnegative. Indeed, write a nonzero rational in lowest terms as \(u/v\), with \(v>0\) and \(\gcd(|u|,v)=1\). If \(v>1\), some prime \(p\) divides \(v\); coprimality implies \(p\nmid u\), so
\(v_p(u/v)=v_p(u)-v_p(v)<0\), a contradiction. Thus \(v=1\). (The zero rational is already an integer.) Applying this criterion to (21) shows that \(A_n\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(n\ge0\).

Since all factors in (1) are positive, these integers are in fact nonnegative. Therefore every coefficient of
\({}_3F_2(2/9,4/9,7/9;1/3,1;729x)\), i.e. every term of A275460, is an integer.
